questions.q: Which of these is the chapter's own description of the barter system?
questions.a: The chapter describes barter as exchanging goods or services directly for other goods or services without money. The other options describe coin payment, deferred payment and storing wheat.
o: Exchanging goods or services directly for other goods or services
Buying goods with coins that a ruler of the kingdom had minted
Taking goods today and promising to make the payment later on
Keeping wheat in a safe store so that it can be used later on

questions.q: Rai stones, giant discs of rock that were used as money, belonged to
questions.a: The chapter places the Rai stones on Yap Island in the Pacific Ocean (Micronesia). The Solomon Islands had the Tevau and Central Mexico the Tajadero.
o: Yap Island in the Pacific Ocean
the Solomon Islands of the Pacific
Central Mexico and Central America
Morigaon district in Assam

questions.q: Which pairing of an unusual form of money with its place is NOT correct according to the chapter?
questions.a: The Tevau, a red feather coil, was used on the Solomon Islands, not on Yap Island, so pairing it with Yap Island is the incorrect one. The other three pairings are as the chapter gives them.
o: Tevau, a coil of red feathers - Yap Island
Rai stones, giant rock discs - Yap Island
Tajadero, a copper chopping knife - Central Mexico
Tevau, a coil of red feathers - Solomon Islands

questions.q: Which of the following did people use as a commodity in barter, according to the chapter?
questions.a: Tea and tobacco are in the chapter's list of commodities. Debit cards, karshapanas and Bank of Bengal notes are later forms of money, not barter commodities.
o: Tea and tobacco
Debit cards and credit cards
Karshapanas punched with rupas
Notes of the Bank of Bengal

questions.q: Mr Nair mends his neighbour's gate and, in return, receives a bag of mangoes from her tree. No rupee changes hands. Which statement fits the chapter's idea of barter?
questions.a: The chapter says barter is the exchange of goods and services, so a service for goods without money is barter. The other options wrongly limit barter to goods, to listed commodities or to equal prices.
o: It is barter, as a service is exchanged for goods without money
It is not barter, as only goods can be exchanged in barter
It is not barter, as mangoes are not on the chapter's list
It is barter only if the mangoes cost as much as the repair

questions.q: Four students describe their Saturday. Shaheen paid ₹30 for samosas. Deepak gave his old comics to a friend and took a puzzle in return. Lata paid her tuition fee by UPI. Gopi received pocket money from his aunt. Whose activity is an example of barter?
questions.a: Only Deepak exchanged one good for another without money. Shaheen used cash, Lata used digital money, and Gopi's pocket money is money received, not an exchange of goods.
o: Deepak's
Shaheen's
Lata's
Gopi's

questions.q:
Read the statements about the barter system and money.
1. The barter system was the earliest form of exchange, and the chapter says there is a lot of evidence of it from around the world.
2. Barter is possible only between people who live in the same village.
3. Money is the common tool that everybody accepts and uses to make or receive payments.
Which of the statements is/are correct?
questions.a: Statements 1 and 3 are from the chapter. Statement 2 is false: the chapter says the distances across which barter took place grew longer, so it was not confined to one village.
o: 1 and 3 only
1 only
2 and 3 only
1, 2 and 3

questions.q:
Assertion (A): The barter system was the earliest form of exchange.
Reason (R): Giant discs of rock called Rai stones were used as money on Yap Island.
Choose the correct option.
questions.a: Both statements are true, but the use of Rai stones on one island does not say anything about which form of exchange came first, so the reason does not explain the assertion.
o: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.q: (a) State the chapter's definition of money. (b) Explain why swapping an extra eraser for an extra pencil does not use money in this sense.
questions.a: (a) Money is the common tool that everybody accepts and uses to make or receive payments in exchange for goods and services. (b) The eraser and pencil are handed over directly for each other, so no common tool of payment is used.
s: Part (a): money as the common tool everybody accepts for making or receiving payments
Part (b): the two goods are exchanged directly, so no payment tool is involved

questions.q: (a) Which form of money was used on Yap Island, and what was it made of? (b) Name the barter problem the chapter calls portability and say why it would trouble a person who owned such money.
questions.a: (a) Rai stones, giant discs of rock. (b) Portability is the ability of an object to be carried from one place to another; giant rock discs are very hard to carry, so the owner could not easily take them where they were needed.
s: Part (a): Rai stones, giant discs of rock
Part (b): portability is ease of carrying, and giant rock discs are hard to carry

questions.q: Differentiate between a commodity and money, giving one example of each from the chapter.
questions.a: A commodity is a product or good that can be traded, bought and sold, for example cattle, salt or tea. Money is the common tool everybody accepts to make or receive payments, for example coins or notes.
s: Commodity: a good that can be traded, with one example from the chapter
Money: the common tool everybody accepts for payment, with one example

questions.q: The chapter's glossary defines both 'transaction' and 'barter system'. Mrs Fernandes tutors a neighbour's child for a month and, in return, receives a sack of rice. Using both terms, explain why this is a transaction and why it is a barter system.
questions.a: A transaction is a piece of business done between people, especially buying or selling. The barter system is exchange of goods and services without money. Tutoring (a service) is exchanged for rice (goods) between two families with no money, so it is a transaction carried out by barter.
s: Transaction is a piece of business between people, especially buying or selling
Barter exchanges goods or services without money, so a service for rice is a transaction done by barter

questions.q: Ranjit's family gives a bag of rice to the village carpenter, who mends their door in return. Identify the goods and the service in this exchange and say why no money is needed.
questions.a: The bag of rice is the goods and the mending of the door is the service. Each side gives what the other wants directly, so no common tool of payment is needed.
s: Rice as the goods and mending the door as the service
Each gives what the other wants directly, so money is not needed

questions.q: Priya says, 'Only everyday things like salt and tea were ever used for exchange; the stone discs of Yap Island were never really accepted by anyone.' Do you agree? Give reasons from the chapter.
questions.a: No. The chapter says Rai stones were used as money on Yap Island, the Tajadero in Central Mexico and the Tevau on the Solomon Islands, so unusual objects were accepted in their regions. Money is whatever people in a place commonly accept for payment, so 'only' is too strong.
s: Verdict: disagrees with the word 'only'
Names at least two unusual forms of money with their places
Links acceptance to the chapter's meaning of money as what everybody accepts

questions.q: Describe a real situation from your school or neighbourhood that is barter. Then change one detail so that it is no longer barter, and explain why it stopped being barter.
questions.a: Example: Asha gives her old story book to Rita and takes Rita's colouring set. If Rita pays ₹40 for the book instead, it is a purchase, because money is now the means of payment and the goods are not swapped directly.
s: Gives a situation in which goods or services are swapped without money
Changes one detail, such as adding a payment in rupees
Explains that barter needs the exchange to be direct, without money

questions.q: Say whether each is barter and give a one-line reason. (i) Arun gives his cousin a cricket ball and takes a chess set. (ii) Arun pays ₹40 for a notebook. (iii) A vendor gives a steel bucket in return for old clothes.
questions.a: (i) Barter, goods are swapped without money. (ii) Not barter, because rupees are the payment. (iii) Barter, because the vendor and household exchange goods without money.
s: (i) barter with the reason that goods are swapped directly
(ii) not barter as money is used
(iii) barter as bucket and clothes are exchanged without money

questions.q: 'There is a lot of evidence of the barter system from around the world.' Justify this statement using the chapter. Include its meaning, the commodities used and the unusual forms of money found in different places.
questions.a: Barter is exchange of goods and services without money, such as mending a gate in return for a bag of mangoes. People used commodities like cowrie shells, salt, tea, tobacco, cloth, cattle (cows, goats, horses, sheep) and seeds. In different parts of the world unusual forms of money were used: Rai stones on Yap Island, the Tajadero in Central Mexico, and the Tevau on the Solomon Islands. Such varied evidence shows that exchange without a common tool was widespread.
s: Defines barter with an example of a service swapped for goods
Lists at least three commodities from the chapter
Names Rai stones with Yap Island
Names the Tajadero and the Tevau with their places
Concludes that the examples come from many parts of the world

questions.q: Anil says, 'Barter means exchange of goods only.' Bela says, 'Barter means exchange without money.' Chitra says, 'Barter means exchange of goods and services without money.' Whose statement matches the chapter, and what is missing from the other two? Support your answer with one example of a service exchanged for goods.
questions.a: Chitra's statement matches the chapter. Anil leaves out services and also leaves out the condition that no money is used, so a swap paid in rupees would fit his words. Bela leaves out that goods and services are the things exchanged. Example: a tailor stitches a blouse for a neighbour and takes a basket of vegetables, which is a service swapped for goods.
s: Identifies Chitra's statement as the chapter's definition
Points out that Anil omits services and the no-money condition
Points out that Bela does not say what is exchanged
Gives a correct example of a service exchanged for goods

questions.q:
Class 7 held a Swap Day on the school lawn and the teacher noted five exchanges.
1. Rhea gave an old atlas and took a puzzle box.
2. Dev paid ₹35 at the stationery stall for a pencil box.
3. Zoya spent two hours helping a friend with homework and took a comic in return.
4. Ishaan gave a cricket glove and received ₹60 from Joy.
5. Neha gave a bag of toffees and took a bookmark.
(a) Which of the five exchanges are barter?
(b) Why is exchange 4 not barter, and what could Joy do to make it barter?
(c) Which exchanges used money, the common tool of payment, and how many rupees changed hands in all?
(d) Next year the committee must choose between 'goods and services only' and 'goods, services and rupee stalls'. Recommend one, giving a reason from the chapter.
questions.a: (a) 1, 3 and 5. (b) Joy paid ₹60, so money was the means of payment; she could give goods or a service that Ishaan wants. (c) Exchanges 2 and 4 used money: ₹35 + ₹60 = ₹95. (d) Either choice is acceptable with a reason: goods and services only keeps the Swap Day purely barter, as in the book exchange club; adding rupee stalls lets people get things without finding someone who wants their goods.
s: Part (a): exchanges 1, 3 and 5 are barter
Part (b): exchange 4 uses money; Joy should give goods or a service instead
Part (c): exchanges 2 and 4 and ₹95
Part (d): a recommendation supported by a reason from the chapter

questions.q:
Arjun wrote three lines in his revision notes for the chapter 'From Barter to Money'.
Line 1: Barter is the exchange of goods and services without money.
Line 2: The Rai stones of Yap Island were a commodity used in barter, not a form of money.
Line 3: Money is the common tool that everybody accepts.
His friend Sana says one line contradicts the chapter and another is incomplete.
(a) Which line contradicts the chapter, and what does the chapter say?
(b) Which line is incomplete, and what is missing from it?
(c) Arjun has room for only one list in his notes: the commodities used in barter, or the three unusual forms of money with their places. Which would help more in an exam answer on 'evidence of barter around the world'? Justify.
questions.a: (a) Line 2 contradicts the chapter, which says Rai stones were used as money on Yap Island. (b) Line 3 is incomplete: it does not say what the common tool is used for, namely to make or receive payments in exchange for goods and services. (c) Either list is acceptable with a reason: the commodity list (cowrie shells, salt, tea, tobacco, cloth, cattle, seeds) shows how many everyday things were used for exchange, while the unusual forms with places show the evidence came from different parts of the world.
s: Part (a): Line 2, since the chapter calls Rai stones money used on Yap Island
Part (b): Line 3, which omits that money is used to make or receive payments for goods and services
Part (c): chooses one list and justifies with its use for the 'around the world' evidence

questions.q: The difficulty of finding a person who wants exactly what you have and who also has exactly what you want is called
questions.a: This is the chapter's double coincidence of wants. The other options are the lack of a common measure of value, divisibility and portability, which are different problems.
o: double coincidence of wants
lack of a common standard measure of value
the problem of divisibility
the problem of portability

questions.q: The farmer cannot keep the wheat he got for his ox for long because it may rot or be eaten by rats. The chapter calls this the problem of
questions.a: Ability to last a long time and withstand damage is durability, and wheat that rots or is eaten fails this. Portability is carrying, divisibility is splitting, and value is the missing common measure.
o: durability
portability
divisibility
common standard measure of value

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT a problem of the barter system discussed in the chapter?
questions.a: A central authority such as the RBI to issue notes belongs to later forms of money, not to the problems of barter. Divisibility, portability and the lack of a measure of value are all barter problems in the chapter.
o: Absence of a central authority like the RBI to print notes
Goods may not be divisible into smaller parts at all
Goods are hard to carry from one place to another
There is no common standard measure of value

questions.q: Salma makes pickles and wants a new school bag for her son. The bag-maker will take only rice, and Salma has none. Which problem of barter has Salma run into?
questions.a: The bag-maker does not want what Salma has, so there is no double coincidence of wants. Pickles are not mentioned as hard to divide, carry or store.
o: Double coincidence of wants
Lack of divisibility
Lack of durability
Lack of portability

questions.q: A potter and a fruit seller both want to swap. The seller offers 4 mangoes for a clay lamp, the potter says the lamp is worth 12 mangoes, and neither can show who is right, so the potter walks away. Which problem is at work?
questions.a: Both want each other's goods, so the trouble is the missing common standard measure of value. The mangoes could spoil, but that is not why they failed to agree.
o: No common standard measure of value
Double coincidence of wants
Lack of durability of the mangoes
Lack of portability of the lamp

questions.q:
Read the statements about the problems of barter.
1. Durability is a problem only for animals such as an ox and never for grains like wheat.
2. Even when two people want each other's goods, deciding the proportion of the exchange can be difficult, as there is no common standard measure of value.
3. A double coincidence of wants is always easy to find, so a person never needs a series of exchanges.
Which of the statements is/are correct?
questions.a: Only statement 2 matches the chapter. Statement 1 is false because the chapter shows wheat rotting or being eaten by rats. Statement 3 is false because the chapter says the farmer might have to go through a series of exchanges.
o: 2 only
1 and 2 only
3 only
1, 2 and 3

questions.q:
Assertion (A): A farmer who wants shoes, a sweater and medicines may need a series of exchanges under barter.
Reason (R): It is unlikely that one person will want his ox and also be able to offer all three things.
Choose the correct option.
questions.a: Both statements are true, and the reason explains why one exchange is not enough: no single person is likely to meet all the farmer's wants.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.q:
Match each problem of barter in Column A with the situation in Column B.
Column A: 1. Double coincidence of wants  2. No common standard measure of value  3. Divisibility  4. Durability
Column B: a. Wheat stored for a season is eaten by rats.  b. Two willing traders cannot agree how many mangoes equal a lamp.  c. A person cannot hand over only a part of an ox for a sweater.  d. The weaver wants wheat but the wheat-owner needs only shoes.
questions.a: Weaver and wheat-owner: double coincidence of wants. Mangoes and lamp: no standard measure of value. Part of an ox: divisibility. Wheat and rats: durability. The distractors swap the two problems about willing traders.

questions.q: (a) A trader stores 30 bags of wheat received in exchange for goods, and rats eat many of them. Name the barter problem. (b) Which function of money named in the chapter would have let him avoid the loss, and how?
questions.a: (a) Durability. (b) Store of value: he could keep money instead of wheat for a longer time and use it for purchases later.
s: Part (a): durability
Part (b): money as a store of value kept instead of wheat for later purchases

questions.q: (a) Explain 'double coincidence of wants' in your own words. (b) Why was it unlikely, in the farmer's story, that a single person would give shoes, a sweater and medicines for one ox?
questions.a: (a) Two people each have something the other wants and can exchange directly. (b) That one person would have to own all three things and also want an ox, which is very unlikely.
s: Part (a): each of the two people has what the other wants
Part (b): one person would need all three items and also want the ox

questions.q: Differentiate between the problem of portability and the problem of durability, with one example of each from the farmer's story.
questions.a: Portability is the ability of an object to be carried from place to place; taking the ox everywhere is the example. Durability is the ability to last and be stored for long; wheat rotting or being eaten by rats is the example.
s: Portability meaning with the ox carried everywhere
Durability meaning with wheat that rots or is eaten by rats

questions.q: What does the chapter mean by a 'common standard measure of value'? Why might a trader refuse an exchange when it is missing?
questions.a: It is an agreed-upon worth that helps decide the value of goods and services. Without it, the trader may feel the exchange is disadvantageous and so would not be interested.
s: Meaning: an agreed worth to determine the value of goods and services
A trader who feels the exchange is disadvantageous refuses it

questions.q: The farmer exchanged his ox for several bags of wheat. Why does the chapter say that this solved only part of his problem?
questions.a: The wheat is easier to divide and handle than an ox, but it still has to be carried to several places and it cannot be stored for long because it rots or is eaten by rats.
s: Wheat helps with dividing and carrying compared with the ox, but must still be transported
Wheat cannot be stored for long since it rots or is eaten by rats

questions.q: Rohit says, 'If two people want each other's goods, the double coincidence of wants is solved, but barter can still fail because they may not agree on how much of one equals the other.' Is he right? Is that the only problem that can remain? Explain with reference to the chapter.
questions.a: Yes, he is right. Even when two people want each other's goods, the chapter says the proportion of the exchange is hard to settle because there is no common standard measure of value. It is not the only problem: goods may not be divisible, as an ox cannot be split to buy a sweater.
s: Verdict: agrees that wanting each other's goods does not settle the proportion
Links the proportion issue to no common standard measure of value
Names a second remaining problem such as divisibility with the ox and sweater

questions.q: Mohan owns one buffalo, worth about 8 sacks of rice. He needs only 1 sack of rice today. Show why he cannot complete this exchange by giving part of his buffalo, name the problem, and say what he would be left with if he gives the whole buffalo.
questions.a: He would have to give one-eighth of the buffalo, which cannot be cut off without destroying its value. This is the problem of divisibility. If he gives the whole buffalo he gets 8 sacks and must carry and store 7 sacks he does not need today, which brings the problems of portability and durability.
s: Shows that only one-eighth of a buffalo would be needed and cannot be separated
Names the problem as divisibility
States that giving the whole buffalo leaves him with 7 extra sacks to carry and store

questions.q: Write a short story of four or five lines about a milk seller in a village where only barter is used, which shows the problem of durability. End with one line on how money would help.
questions.a: Example: Kamla gets a sack of grain from the weaver for her milk, but the next day the milk she was keeping for another trader has gone sour, and she cannot keep the grain safe from rats. With money she could sell the milk at once and keep the rupees to spend later.
s: A story where a good is spoilt or damaged while being kept
The spoilage is clearly the problem of durability
One line saying money can be kept and used later

questions.q: A farmer has one ox and needs shoes, a sweater and medicines for his grandmother. Show how each of the five problems of barter that the chapter lists appears in his situation.
questions.a: Double coincidence of wants: he must find someone who wants an ox and offers what he needs. No common standard measure of value: it is hard to decide how much wheat equals shoes or a sweater. Divisibility: he cannot exchange a part of an ox for a sweater. Portability: taking the ox everywhere is difficult. Durability: the wheat he gets in exchange rots or is eaten by rats.
s: Double coincidence of wants shown in the search for a person who wants the ox
No common standard measure of value in deciding the amount of wheat for each item
Divisibility with a part of an ox for a sweater
Portability with carrying the ox or the wheat from place to place
Durability with stored wheat rotting or eaten by rats

questions.q: 'Money makes the farmer's situation easier.' Justify this statement by choosing any three problems of barter and explaining how money removes each one. Then show how the farmer would complete his shopping for shoes, a sweater and medicines using money.
questions.a: Double coincidence of wants: money is accepted by everybody, so he need not find someone who wants an ox. Common standard measure of value: prices in money let the ox, shoes and sweater be compared. Portability and durability: money is easy to carry and can be kept for a long time instead of rotting wheat. Shopping: he sells the ox for money, then pays the cobbler, the weaver and the chemist separately and keeps what remains for later.
s: First problem with how money removes it
Second problem with how money removes it
Third problem with how money removes it
Describes selling the ox for money
Describes paying the three sellers one by one and keeping the rest

questions.q:
At the Dindori weekly market, Bhima has one goat and wants shoes, a sweater and medicines. In barter, the traders' rates are 15 kg of wheat for the shoes, 20 kg for the sweater and 5 kg for the medicines. A grain trader offers 70 kg of wheat for the goat, while a cattle dealer offers ₹2,400 in cash. Wheat sells at ₹30 per kg in the market.
(a) After buying all three things with wheat, how many kilograms of wheat will Bhima still have?
(b) Name the two barter problems that this leftover wheat will give him.
(c) If he takes the ₹6,000 and pays the traders the rupee value of the same wheat rates, how much money is left, and how does that compare with the value of the leftover wheat?
(d) Recommend whether Bhima should accept the wheat or the cash offer, giving a reason from the chapter.
questions.a: (a) 70 - (15 + 20 + 5) = 30 kg. (b) Portability, since he has to carry it, and durability, since it can rot or be eaten by rats. (c) The three items cost 40 kg x ₹30 = ₹1,200, so ₹1,200 is left from the ₹2,400; the leftover wheat is worth 30 x ₹30 = ₹900, which is ₹300 less. (d) Either choice is acceptable with a reason: cash can be kept as a store of value and is easy to carry and is worth ₹300 more, but the wheat offer suits him only if he can use or sell the wheat soon.
s: Part (a): 30 kg of wheat left
Part (b): portability and durability
Part (c): ₹1,200 left against wheat worth ₹900
Part (d): a recommendation justified by store of value or the ₹300 difference

questions.q:
At a village haat, Lata has one sealed sack of rice worth ₹800 and no other goods. Gopal has an oil lamp worth ₹500 and wants cloth. Farida has one stitched shawl worth ₹800 and wants rice. The sack must be taken whole, the shawl cannot be cut and the lamp cannot be split. A trader at the haat is ready to buy the sack for ₹800 in cash.
(a) Can Lata and Gopal complete a direct swap? Give the reason.
(b) Describe a chain of two exchanges after which Lata has the lamp.
(c) In that chain Lata hands over the shawl worth ₹800 for a lamp worth ₹500. Which barter problem stops Gopal from giving back the extra value, and how much does Lata lose?
(d) Lata could instead sell the sack to the trader for ₹800 and pay Gopal ₹500 for the lamp. Compare the two routes and recommend one.
questions.a: (a) No, Gopal wants cloth, not rice. (b) Lata gives her sack to Farida and takes the shawl, then gives the shawl to Gopal and takes the lamp. (c) Divisibility: the lamp (and the shawl) cannot be split to return the difference, and Gopal has nothing else to give; she loses ₹800 - ₹500 = ₹300 of value. (d) With rupees she pays ₹500 for the lamp and keeps ₹300, while the chain loses ₹300 of value, so the money route is better.
s: Part (a): no, since Gopal wants cloth and not rice
Part (b): sack to Farida for the shawl, then shawl to Gopal for the lamp
Part (c): divisibility and a loss of ₹300
Part (d): money route keeps ₹300 against a loss of ₹300 in the chain

questions.q: In the name of the Junbeel Mela, the Assamese word 'beel' means
questions.a: The chapter gives jun as moon and beel as wetland. Fire and fair are not parts of the name; fire belongs to the Agni Puja.
o: wetland
the moon
a fire
a fair

questions.q: The Junbeel Mela begins with
questions.a: The mela begins with the Agni Puja, the worship of fire, a prayer for universal wellbeing. The moon is only in the meaning of 'jun', and bartering starts later, early in the morning.
o: the Agni Puja, worship of fire
a prayer to the moon over the wetland
a meeting of the Tiwa chiefs alone
the first round of bartering at dawn

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT true of the Junbeel Mela as described in the chapter?
questions.a: It is a three-day annual fair, not a daily market. The other statements are as the chapter gives them: held at Junbeel in Morigaon district, barter early in the morning, and hill goods exchanged for rice cakes.
o: It is a daily market where every trade is done in rupees
It is a three-day annual fair held at Junbeel in Morigaon district
Bartering of local products begins early in the morning
Hill goods are exchanged for rice cakes and other foods

questions.q: Which of these is given in the chapter as an example of barter that continues today?
questions.a: The chapter describes a club where friends swap books they have read. A QR code, UPI and Roman gold coins are digital money and coinage, not barter.
o: A book club where friends swap books
A QR code card kept on a fruit seller's cart
A bank transfer of money made through UPI
Roman gold coins dug up at Pudukkottai site

questions.q: A vendor comes to Mrs Reddy's flat with steel plates and offers one for her old sarees. What does the vendor gain from this exchange, according to the chapter?
questions.a: The vendor collects used cloth that can be resold, repurposed or recycled. A bank payment, fair profit share or utensil price rise is not part of the chapter's explanation.
o: Cloth to resell, repurpose or recycle
A digital payment sent into her bank account
A share of the profit from the next big fair
A rise in the price of steel utensils sold

questions.q: A hill family brings handmade baskets, made from forest materials, to the Junbeel Mela, where people from the plains also arrive. What is it most likely to take back?
questions.a: The chapter says handmade goods from the hills are exchanged with people from the plains for rice cakes and other foods that cannot be grown in the hills. The other options reverse the exchange or bring in rupees.
o: Rice cakes and other foods not grown in hills
Roots, fruit and spices that grow in its own hills
Old clothes that are traded for new steel utensils
Rupee notes at a rate that the chiefs have fixed

questions.q:
Read the statements about barter today.
1. The Junbeel Mela grew from yearly gatherings of the chiefs of the Tiwa, Karbi, Khasi and Jaintia communities, which began in the 15th century.
2. At the Junbeel Mela, hill people exchange handmade goods for rice cakes and other foods that cannot be grown in the hills.
3. Since money has replaced barter around the world, no barter can be seen anywhere today.
Which of the statements is/are correct?
questions.a: Statements 1 and 2 are from the chapter. Statement 3 is false: the chapter says some barter systems still exist, such as the Junbeel Mela.
o: 1 and 2 only
2 and 3 only
1 only
1, 2 and 3

questions.q:
Assertion (A): The Junbeel Mela is described as a socio-cultural fair.
Reason (R): Bartering of roots, vegetables, fruit, herbs and spices begins early in the morning at the mela.
Choose the correct option.
questions.a: Both are true, but the early-morning bartering does not explain why the fair is called socio-cultural; that comes from the gatherings of chiefs and the Agni Puja.
o: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.

questions.q:

A quarter-anna is one-fourth of an anna and a half-anna is half of an anna. The chapter says that 1 anna was 1/16 of a rupee and in 1947 one anna could buy a dozen bananas. (b) What fraction of a rupee is that?

questions.q:

(b) So, to the nearest kilogram, how much grain was one pana worth?
(c) How many times the annual salary of 60 panas was the fine?
(d) One reader says the fine was meant to raise money for the ruler. Another says it was meant to make people value helping neighbours. Which reading do your figures support better? Name one further piece of evidence that would help.
questions.a: (a) 365 x 3 = 1,095 kg. (b) 1,095 / 60 = 18.25, about 18 kg. (c) 100 / 60, about 1.7 times. (d) The fine was larger than a whole year's salary, which fits the idea that helping a neighbour was valued; to be sure, one would want to know whether the fines were actually collected or what the ruler did with them.
s: Part (a): 1,095 kg
Part (b): about 18 kg
Part (c): about 1.7 times
Part (d): a reading supported by the figures plus one useful extra evidence

Either decision is acceptable with a reason: keep accepting cash so that 40% of customers are not lost, or move to QR only if the 24% of takings is outweighed by convenience.

questions.q:
Mohan Lal's grocery shop in Jaipur received ₹5,00,000 last month. Of this, ₹3,20,000 came through QR-code payments straight into his bank account and the rest was cash, all in ₹500 notes. His supplier must be paid ₹4,00,000 by bank transfer on the 5th.
(a) How much cash did he receive, what percentage of the month's money came by QR code, and is a QR payment tangible or intangible money?
(b) How much of his cash must he deposit in the bank to be able to transfer ₹4,00,000?
(c) How many ₹500 notes make up that deposit? How many ₹10 coins would the same deposit need?
(d) He can deposit that cash and transfer the whole amount, or hand the supplier that cash directly and transfer the rest. Recommend one, giving a reason from the chapter about carrying and storing many notes or about money moving directly between bank accounts.
questions.a: (a) ₹5,00,000 - ₹3,20,000 = ₹1,80,000 cash; QR share 3,20,000 / 5,00,000 = 64%; a QR payment is intangible (digital) money. (b) ₹4,00,000 - ₹3,20,000 = ₹80,000. (c) 80,000 / 500 = 160 notes; in ₹10 coins it would need 8,000 coins. (d) Either choice is acceptable with a reason from the chapter: depositing and transferring moves money directly between bank accounts and nothing has to be carried, while handing over cash means carrying and storing 160 notes, the kind of difficulty that led away from coins and towards paper and digital money.
s: Part (a): ₹1,80,000, 64% and intangible (digital)
Part (c): 160 notes against 8,000 coins
Part (d): a recommendation with a chapter reason about carrying cash or direct bank-to-bank transfer
